claim: Lagging chromosome is a hallmark of aneuploidy arising from errors in the kinetochore–spindle attachment in animal cells.
source: Lagging chromosome is a hallmark of aneuploidy arising from errors in the kinetochore–spindle attachment in animal cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about animal cells in the abstract.

claim: Kinetochore components and cellular phenotypes associated with kinetochore dysfunction are much less explored in plants.
source: However, kinetochore components and cellular phenotypes associated with kinetochore dysfunction are much less explored in plants.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Knock-down of several kinetochore proteins led to polyploidy, not aneuploidy, through cytokinesis failure in >90% of the cells that exhibited lagging chromosomes for several minutes or longer.
source: Most surprisingly, knock-down of several kinetochore proteins led to polyploidy, not aneuploidy, through cytokinesis failure in >90% of the cells that exhibited lagging chromosomes for several minutes or longer.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study presented in the abstract, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The resultant cells containing two or more nuclei proceeded to the next cell cycle and eventually developed into polyploid plants.
source: The resultant cells, containing two or more nuclei, proceeded to the next cell cycle and eventually developed into polyploid plants.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study presented in the abstract, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lagging chromosomes have been observed in various plant species in the wild.
source: As lagging chromosomes have been observed in various plant species in the wild, our observation raised a possibility that they could be one of the natural pathways to polyploidy in plants.
evidence: This is stated as existing knowledge in the abstract and later supported by citations in the discussion.

claim: Lagging chromosomes could be one of the natural pathways to polyploidy in plants.
source: As lagging chromosomes have been observed in various plant species in the wild, our observation raised a possibility that they could be one of the natural pathways to polyploidy in plants.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and existing observations.

claim: Most of our knowledge on kinetochore function and impact on genome stability is derived from animal and yeast studies.
source: Most of our knowledge on kinetochore function and impact on genome stability is derived from animal and yeast studies (Musacchio and Desai, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Plants possess conserved kinetochore proteins.
source: Another major group of eukaryotes, plants, also possesses conserved kinetochore proteins (Yu et al., 2000; van Hooff et al., 2017; Yamada and Goshima, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: 12 out of 16 components that form CCAN in animal and yeast cells cannot be identified by homology searches in plants.
source: For example, 12 out of 16 components that form CCAN (constitutive centromere associated network) in animal and yeast cells cannot be identified by homology searches (Musacchio and Desai, 2017; Yamada and Goshima, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The majority of P. patens tissues are in a haploid state.
source: The majority of its tissues are in a haploid state, and, owing to an extremely high rate of homologous recombination, gene disruption and fluorescent protein tagging of endogenous genes are easy to obtain in the first generation (Cove et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about P. patens supported by a citation.

claim: P. patens has an extremely high rate of homologous recombination.
source: The majority of its tissues are in a haploid state, and, owing to an extremely high rate of homologous recombination, gene disruption and fluorescent protein tagging of endogenous genes are easy to obtain in the first generation (Cove et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about P. patens supported by a citation.

claim: All the P. patens proteins identified as the homologue of human kinetochore components are conserved in A. thaliana.
source: The homology search indicated that all the P. patens proteins identified as the homologue of human kinetochore components are conserved in the most popular model plant species A. thaliana (Yamada and Goshima, 2017): therefore, the knowledge gained in P. patens would be largely applicable to flowering plants, including crop species.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from homology search supported by a citation.

claim: Knowledge gained in P. patens would be largely applicable to flowering plants, including crop species.
source: The homology search indicated that all the P. patens proteins identified as the homologue of human kinetochore components are conserved in the most popular model plant species A. thaliana (Yamada and Goshima, 2017): therefore, the knowledge gained in P. patens would be largely applicable to flowering plants, including crop species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of kinetochore proteins.

claim: P. patens differentiated gametophore leaf cells, when excised, are efficiently reprogrammed to become stem cells.
source: Another remarkable feature of P. patens is its regeneration ability; for example, differentiated gametophore leaf cells, when excised, are efficiently reprogrammed to become stem cells (Sato et al., 2017; Ishikawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about P. patens supported by citations.

claim: Genome alteration even in a somatic cell can potentially spread through the population in P. patens.
source: Thus, genome alteration even in a somatic cell can potentially spread through the population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the regeneration ability of P. patens.

claim: A fluorescent tag was inserted in-frame at the N- and/or C-terminus of 18 selected kinetochore proteins.
source: To observe the endogenous localization of putative kinetochore components, we inserted a fluorescent tag in-frame at the N- and/or C-terminus of 18 selected proteins, which contain at least one subunit per sub-complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: For 10 proteins, function was unlikely perturbed by tagging, as the transgenic moss grew indistinguishably from wild-type.
source: For 10 proteins, function was unlikely perturbed by tagging, as the transgenic moss grew indistinguishably from wild-type, despite the single-copy protein being replaced with the tagged protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The C-terminal tagging line for CENP-S could not be obtained after two attempts, suggesting that tagging affected the protein's function and thereby moss viability.
source: The C-terminal tagging line for CENP-S could not be obtained after two attempts, suggesting that tagging affected the protein's function and thereby moss viability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure to obtain a tagging line.

claim: Many of the proteins were localized to the kinetochore at least transiently during the cell cycle.
source: Consistent with their sequence homology, many of the proteins were localized to the kinetochore at least transiently during the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a finding from the localization analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Multiple proteins showed unexpected localization (or disappearance) at certain cell cycle stages.
source: However, multiple proteins also showed unexpected localization (or disappearance) at certain cell cycle stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2–7; Videos 1–4).
evidence: This is a finding from the localization analysis shown in supplementary figures and videos.

claim: CENP-X, CENP-O and CENP-S did not show kinetochore enrichment at any stages.
source: Most surprising were CCAN protein dynamics: CENP-X, CENP-O and CENP-S did not show kinetochore enrichment at any stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Videos 1 and 3), whereas CENP-C also dissociated from the kinetochore transiently in the post-mitotic phase (Figure 1B−Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the localization analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Videos 1 and 3.

claim: CENP-C dissociated from the kinetochore transiently in the post-mitotic phase.
source: Most surprising were CCAN protein dynamics: CENP-X, CENP-O and CENP-S did not show kinetochore enrichment at any stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Videos 1 and 3), whereas CENP-C also dissociated from the kinetochore transiently in the post-mitotic phase (Figure 1B−Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the localization analysis shown in Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: No 'constitutive' kinetochore proteins other than CENP-A could be identified.
source: Thus, we could not identify any 'constitutive' kinetochore proteins other than CENP-A.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization analysis data.

claim: Knockout lines and/or frameshift mutation using CRISPR/Cas9 could not be obtained for the single-copy kinetochore proteins, except for Mad2.
source: We failed to obtain knockout lines and/or induce frameshift mutation using CRISPR/Cas9 for the single-copy kinetochore proteins, except for the spindle checkpoint protein Mad2, strongly suggesting that they are essential for moss viability.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental attempts.

claim: Single-copy kinetochore proteins (except Mad2) are essential for moss viability.
source: We failed to obtain knockout lines and/or induce frameshift mutation using CRISPR/Cas9 for the single-copy kinetochore proteins, except for the spindle checkpoint protein Mad2, strongly suggesting that they are essential for moss viability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure to obtain knockout lines.

claim: Mitotic defects were observed in multiple RNAi lines, such as delay in mitotic progression, chromosome missegregation and/or multi-nuclei.
source: We observed mitotic defects in multiple RNAi lines, such as delay in mitotic progression, chromosome missegregation and/or multi-nuclei; these phenotypes were never observed in the control line (Figure 2A,B; Video 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2A,B and Video 5.

claim: Mitotic defects were never observed in the control line.
source: We observed mitotic defects in multiple RNAi lines, such as delay in mitotic progression, chromosome missegregation and/or multi-nuclei; these phenotypes were never observed in the control line (Figure 2A,B; Video 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiments shown in Figure 2A,B and Video 5.

claim: A significant mitotic delay and chromosome alignment/segregation defects were observed in the CENP-A RNAi lines.
source: As expected, we observed a significant mitotic delay and chromosome alignment/segregation defects in the CENP-A RNAi lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the CENP-A RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Video 6.

claim: Micronuclei were occasionally observed in the daughter cells after CENP-A RNAi.
source: Consequently, micronuclei were occasionally observed in the daughter cells, a hallmark of aneuploidy.
evidence: This is a finding from the CENP-A RNAi experiments.

claim: CENP-A is essential for equal chromosome segregation during mitosis in moss.
source: We concluded that CENP-A, like in many organisms, is essential for equal chromosome segregation during mitosis in moss.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CENP-A RNAi experimental data.

claim: Cells with two large nuclei were frequently observed in CENP-A RNAi lines.
source: Surprisingly, we also frequently observed cells with two large nuclei in both RNAi lines (Figures 2B at 1 h 18 min), which is the typical outcome of cytokinesis failure in this cell type (Kosetsu et al., 2013; Miki et al., 2014; Naito and Goshima, 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the CENP-A RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2B, supported by citations about cytokinesis failure.

claim: Mitotic delay and chromosome missegregation were observed in the SKA1 RNAi line.
source: As expected, mitotic delay and chromosome missegregation were observed in the RNAi line (Figure 2B−Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the SKA1 RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Video 5.

claim: Cytokinesis failure was detected in the SKA1 RNAi line.
source: In addition, cytokinesis failure was also detected (Figure 2B; Video 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the SKA1 RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2B and Video 7.

claim: Ectopically expressed RNAi-insensitive SKA1-Cerulean rescued all the phenotypes in the SKA1 RNAi line.
source: To verify that the observed phenotype of SKA1 was not due to an off-target effect, we ectopically expressed RNAi-insensitive SKA1-Cerulean in the RNAi line and observed the rescue of all the above phenotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the rescue experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar phenotypes were observed in RNAi lines targeting CENP-C, Nnf1, KNL1 and Nuf2.
source: Furthermore, we observed a similar phenotype in RNAi lines targeting CENP-C (CCAN), Nnf1 (Mis12 complex), KNL1 and Nuf2 (Ndc80 complex), suggesting that cytokinesis failure is a common outcome following kinetochore malfunction (Figure 2; Video 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2 and Video 5.

claim: Cytokinesis failure is a common outcome following kinetochore malfunction.
source: Furthermore, we observed a similar phenotype in RNAi lines targeting CENP-C (CCAN), Nnf1 (Mis12 complex), KNL1 and Nuf2 (Ndc80 complex), suggesting that cytokinesis failure is a common outcome following kinetochore malfunction (Figure 2; Video 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of similar phenotypes across multiple RNAi lines.

claim: CENP-X RNAi lines showed similar phenotypes to CENP-A and SKA1, including cytokinesis failure.
source: Interestingly, we observed similar phenotypes to CENP-A and SKA1, including cytokinesis failure (Figure 2B−Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the CENP-X RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Video 6.

claim: CENP-X RNAi phenotypes were rescued by the ectopic expression of CENP-X-Cerulean that was resistant to the RNAi construct.
source: CENP-X RNAi phenotypes were rescued by the ectopic expression of CENP-X-Cerulean that was resistant to the RNAi construct (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the rescue experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CENP-X has lost its kinetochore localization in moss, but is still essential for chromosome segregation and cell division.
source: Thus, CENP-X has lost its kinetochore localization in moss, but is still essential for chromosome segregation and cell division.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization and RNAi experimental data.

claim: A minor delay of chromosomes in the midzone (<4 min) never perturbed cytokinesis.
source: Interestingly, a minor delay of chromosomes in the midzone (<4 min) never perturbed cytokinesis (100%, n = 9 for CENP-A, n = 4 for CENP-X and n = 3 for SKA1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of lagging chromosomes and cytokinesis.

claim: If a longer delay of chromosome clearance from the midzone was observed, cytokinesis defects occurred in 96% of the cells.
source: By contrast, if we observed a longer delay of chromosome clearance from the midzone, even when only a single chromosome was detectable, cytokinesis defects occurred in 96% of the cells (n = 9, 14 and 5; Figure 2C,D−Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of lagging chromosomes and cytokinesis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Microtubules reorganized into phragmoplast-like structures upon chromosome segregation in every cell, regardless of the severity of chromosome missegregation.
source: We observed that microtubules reorganized into phragmoplast-like structures upon chromosome segregation in every cell, regardless of the severity of chromosome missegregation (e.g. 32 min in Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the high-resolution imaging shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Microtubule interdigitates at the phragmoplast midzone were abnormal in the kinetochore RNAi lines.
source: However, high-resolution imaging showed that microtubule interdigitates at the phragmoplast midzone were abnormal in the kinetochore RNAi lines.
evidence: This is a finding from the high-resolution imaging.

claim: In 5 out of 7 control cells, a sharp microtubule overlap indicated by bright GFP-tubulin signals was observed during cytokinesis.
source: In 5 out of 7 control cells, a sharp microtubule overlap indicated by bright GFP-tubulin signals was observed during cytokinesis, as expected from previous studies (Kosetsu et al., 2013; Hiwatashi et al., 2008) (yellow arrowhead in Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the high-resolution imaging shown in Figure 2E, supported by citations.

claim: CENP-A and SKA1 RNAi lines that had lagging chromosomes and eventually failed cytokinesis never exhibited focused microtubule overlaps.
source: In contrast, CENP-A and SKA1 RNAi lines that had lagging chromosomes and eventually failed cytokinesis never exhibited such focused overlaps (0 out of 12 cells); instead, the overlap was broader and less distinguished (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the high-resolution imaging shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The cell plate did not form in the cells that had lagging chromosomes for a long time.
source: We could not observe vesicle fusion at the midzone following anaphase onset; thus, the cell plate did not form in the cells that had lagging chromosomes for a long time (Figure 2B,E; Video 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the FM4-64 dye experiments shown in Figure 2B,E and Video 8.

claim: Occupation of the midzone by lagging chromosomes for several minutes prevents proper phragmoplast assembly and cell plate formation, which subsequently causes cytokinesis failure.
source: From these results, we concluded that occupation of the midzone by lagging chromosomes for several minutes prevents proper phragmoplast assembly and cell plate formation, which subsequently causes cytokinesis failure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data on lagging chromosomes, phragmoplast assembly, and cell plate formation.

claim: The majority of the multi-nucleated cells after CENP-A RNAi underwent DNA replication and became tetraploid or attained even higher ploidy.
source: We observed that the majority of the multi-nucleated cells after CENP-A RNAi underwent DNA replication and became tetraploid or attained even higher ploidy (Figure 3A; DNA was quantified at day 5 after β-estradiol treatment).
evidence: This is a finding from the DNA content quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 10% or 25% multi-nucleated apical cells executed the next cell division by forming a single spindle.
source: During the imaging period, we indeed observed cytokinesis failure and 10% or 25% multi-nucleated apical cells executed the next cell division by forming a single spindle (n = 43 and 25 for experiments 1 and 2, respectively, Figure 3B; Video 9).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the long-term time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3B and Video 9.

claim: Cells that have undergone cytokinesis failure can continue cell cycling as diploids at a certain probability.
source: Nevertheless, this data strongly suggests that cells that have undergone cytokinesis failure can continue cell cycling as diploids at a certain probability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the long-term time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Diploid P. patens is known to develop protonema tissue with a few gametophores.
source: Diploid P. patens is known to develop protonema tissue with a few gametophores (leafy shoots) (Schween et al., 2005); therefore, a multi-nucleated cell produced by the cytokinesis failure of a caulonemal cell might proliferate and form a large protonema colony.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A multi-nucleated cell produced by the cytokinesis failure of a caulonemal cell might proliferate and form a large protonema colony.
source: Diploid P. patens is known to develop protonema tissue with a few gametophores (leafy shoots) (Schween et al., 2005); therefore, a multi-nucleated cell produced by the cytokinesis failure of a caulonemal cell might proliferate and form a large protonema colony.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known characteristics of diploid P. patens.

claim: Four moss colonies were obtained after 6 weeks of culturing isolated cells without β-estradiol.
source: After 6 weeks of culturing without β-estradiol (i.e. RNAi was turned off), we obtained four moss colonies, two of which consisted mainly of protonemal cells with a few gametophores (Figure 3D, colony 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell isolation and regeneration experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Two of the four regenerated colonies consisted mainly of protonemal cells with a few gametophores.
source: After 6 weeks of culturing without β-estradiol (i.e. RNAi was turned off), we obtained four moss colonies, two of which consisted mainly of protonemal cells with a few gametophores (Figure 3D, colony 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell isolation and regeneration experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The majority of the cells derived from two colonies had DNA content approximately double of the control haploid cells.
source: DNA staining and quantification showed that the majority of the cells derived from those two colonies had DNA content approximately double of the control haploid cells, which were regenerated in an identical manner (Figure 3E, colony 3 and 4, regenerated from cell 3 and 4, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the DNA content quantification shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A polyploid plant was regenerated from a single multi-nucleated somatic cell.
source: Thus, a polyploid plant was regenerated from a single multi-nucleated somatic cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the single-cell isolation and DNA content quantification data.

claim: The behavior of outer kinetochore subunits was largely consistent with their animal counterparts, suggesting that the mitotic function is also conserved.
source: Overall, the behavior of outer subunits was largely consistent with their animal counterparts, suggesting that the mitotic function is also conserved.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization analysis data.

claim: The timing of kinetochore enrichment differed from that of animal cells and even flowering plants.
source: However, the timing of kinetochore enrichment differed from that of animal cells and even flowering plants (e.g. Arabidopsis, maize) (Shin et al., 2018; Du and Dawe, 2007; Hori et al., 2003): for example, P. patens Ndc80 complex gradually accumulated at the kinetochore after NEBD, unlike Arabidopsis and maize, where it showed kinetochore enrichment throughout the cell cycle (Shin et al., 2018; Du and Dawe, 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from the localization analysis, compared with cited studies.

claim: P. patens Ndc80 complex gradually accumulated at the kinetochore after NEBD.
source: However, the timing of kinetochore enrichment differed from that of animal cells and even flowering plants (e.g. Arabidopsis, maize) (Shin et al., 2018; Du and Dawe, 2007; Hori et al., 2003): for example, P. patens Ndc80 complex gradually accumulated at the kinetochore after NEBD, unlike Arabidopsis and maize, where it showed kinetochore enrichment throughout the cell cycle (Shin et al., 2018; Du and Dawe, 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from the localization analysis.

claim: In Arabidopsis and maize, Ndc80 showed kinetochore enrichment throughout the cell cycle.
source: However, the timing of kinetochore enrichment differed from that of animal cells and even flowering plants (e.g. Arabidopsis, maize) (Shin et al., 2018; Du and Dawe, 2007; Hori et al., 2003): for example, P. patens Ndc80 complex gradually accumulated at the kinetochore after NEBD, unlike Arabidopsis and maize, where it showed kinetochore enrichment throughout the cell cycle (Shin et al., 2018; Du and Dawe, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: CENP-C disappeared from the centromeres shortly after mitotic exit.
source: For example, CENP-C disappeared from the centromeres shortly after mitotic exit.
evidence: This is a finding from the localization analysis.

claim: In animal cells, CENP-C has been suggested to act in cooperation with Mis18BP1/KNL2 to facilitate CENP-A deposition in late telophase and early G1.
source: In animal cells, CENP-C has been suggested to act in cooperation with Mis18BP1/KNL2 to facilitate CENP-A deposition in late telophase and early G1 (2).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from animal cell studies (note: citation appears incomplete in manuscript).

claim: The mechanism of CENP-A incorporation might have been modified in plants.
source: Hence, the mechanism of CENP-A incorporation might have been modified in plants.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed differences in CENP-C localization.

claim: In human cells, 16 CCAN subunits, forming four sub-complexes, have been identified and shown to be critical for kinetochore assembly and function.
source: In human cells, 16 CCAN subunits, forming four sub-complexes, have been identified and shown to be critical for kinetochore assembly and function, not only in cells, but also in reconstitution systems (Guse et al., 2011; Weir et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from human cell studies supported by citations.

claim: In plants, only four CCAN homologues have been identified through sequence homology search.
source: In plants, only four CCAN homologues have been identified through sequence homology search.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The complete lack of kinetochore localization for CENP-O, -S, -X suggests that plants have lost the entire kinetochore-enriched CCAN complex.
source: However, the complete lack of kinetochore localization for CENP-O, -S, -X suggests that plants have lost the entire kinetochore-enriched CCAN complex.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the localization data.

claim: In animals, it has been proposed that CENP-S and CENP-X form a complex and play an important role in outer kinetochore assembly.
source: In animals, it has been proposed that CENP-S and CENP-X form a complex and play an important role in outer kinetochore assembly (Amano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from animal studies supported by a citation.

claim: Lagging chromosomes and cytokinesis failure were observed after knocking down kinetochore components.
source: We observed lagging chromosomes as well as cytokinesis failure after knocking down kinetochore components.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Failure in chromosome separation/segregation and cytokinesis can be caused by a single gene mutation, if the gene has multiple functions.
source: Failure in chromosome separation/segregation and cytokinesis can be caused by a single gene mutation, if the gene has multiple functions; for example, separase Rsw4 (radially swollen4) in A. thaliana is involved in sister chromatid separation, cyclin B turnover and vesicle trafficking that is required for phragmoplast formation (Chang et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2011; Moschou et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Both phenotypes (chromosome missegregation and cytokinesis failure) were observed after RNAi treatment of CENP-A, a constitutive centromeric histone protein that is unlikely to play a direct role in cytokinesis.
source: By contrast, in our study, both phenotypes were observed after RNAi treatment of CENP-A, a constitutive centromeric histone protein that is unlikely to play a direct role in cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a finding from the CENP-A RNAi experiments.

claim: The cytokinesis phenotype frequently appeared in RNAi lines targeting six kinetochore proteins, and only when lagging chromosomes were present.
source: Furthermore, the cytokinesis phenotype frequently appeared in RNAi lines targeting other six kinetochore proteins, and only when lagging chromosomes were present.
evidence: This is a finding from the RNAi experiments.

claim: Persistent lagging chromosomes cause cytokinesis failure.
source: Based on these data, we propose that persistent lagging chromosomes cause cytokinesis failure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Lagging chromosomes might act as physical obstacles to perturb phragmoplast microtubule amplification and/or cell plate formation.
source: Lagging chromosomes might act as physical obstacles to perturb phragmoplast microtubule amplification and/or cell plate formation.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observed phenotypes.

claim: Persistent lagging chromosomes might produce an unknown signal or induce a certain cell state that inhibits phragmoplast expansion and/or cell plate formation in order to prevent chromosome damage.
source: Alternatively, persistent lagging chromosomes might produce an unknown signal or induce a certain cell state that inhibits phragmoplast expansion and/or cell plate formation in order to prevent chromosome damage, reminiscent of the NoCut pathway in animal cytokinesis (Norden et al., 2006; Amaral et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observed phenotypes, with reference to a similar pathway in animal cells.

claim: Abnormal microtubule interdigitates were observed in the whole phragmoplast and not limited to the region proximal to the lagging chromosome.
source: We favor the latter model, as abnormal microtubule interdigitates were observed in the whole phragmoplast and not limited to the region proximal to the lagging chromosome (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the high-resolution imaging shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In a recent study, cytokinesis in moss protonema cells could be completed despite longer microtubule overlaps.
source: Notably, in a recent study, cytokinesis in moss protonema cells could be completed despite longer microtubule overlaps (de Keijzer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Abnormal microtubule interdigitates represent the consequence of microtubule dynamics mis-regulation rather than the direct cause of cytokinesis failure.
source: It suggests that abnormal microtubule interdigitates represent the consequence of microtubule dynamics mis-regulation rather than the direct cause of cytokinesis failure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study and the observed data.

claim: In P. patens, chromosome missegregation in a single cell could lead to the generation of polyploid plants.
source: Our data further suggest that, in P. patens, chromosome missegregation in a single cell could lead to the generation of polyploid plants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: In control moss cells, no lagging chromosome could be found, since mitotic fidelity is very high in culture conditions.
source: In our imaging of control moss cells, we could not find any lagging chromosome, since mitotic fidelity is very high in our culture conditions.
evidence: This is an observation from the control experiments.

claim: Various mitotic abnormalities, including lagging chromosomes have been long observed in wild-type plants and crops, albeit at a low frequency and/or under harsh natural conditions.
source: Intriguingly, however, various mitotic abnormalities, including lagging chromosomes have been long observed in wild-type plants and crops, albeit at a low frequency and/or under harsh natural conditions (Menéndez-Yuffá et al., 2000; Nichols, 1941; Kvitko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The presence of lagging chromosomes for a certain duration is expected to similarly perturb cytokinesis in flowering plants as observed in moss.
source: Those studies did not analyze the relationship between lagging chromosomes and cytokinesis integrity; we expect the presence of lagging chromosomes for a certain duration to similarly perturb cytokinesis as observed in our study of moss, since the cytokinesis process is highly conserved between bryophytes and angiosperms (Smertenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the conservation of cytokinesis processes, supported by a citation.

claim: The cytokinesis process is highly conserved between bryophytes and angiosperms.
source: Those studies did not analyze the relationship between lagging chromosomes and cytokinesis integrity; we expect the presence of lagging chromosomes for a certain duration to similarly perturb cytokinesis as observed in our study of moss, since the cytokinesis process is highly conserved between bryophytes and angiosperms (Smertenko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Genome sequencing suggests that P. patens experienced whole genome duplication at least once during evolution.
source: Genome sequencing suggests that P. patens, like many other plant species, experienced whole genome duplication at least once during evolution (Rensing et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Polyploidization through spontaneous mitotic errors in somatic cells might have a greater impact on de novo formation of polyploid plants than previously anticipated.
source: Polyploidization through spontaneous mitotic errors in somatic cells might have a greater impact on de novo formation of polyploid plants than previously anticipated.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and evolutionary context.
